blocks.text: It is still HTML, CSS and JavaScript served from a URL. Three additions change how it behaves: a **manifest** file tells the phone how to install it, a **service worker** script lets it open with no connection, and the **Push API** lets your server wake it up to show a notification.
Try the phone on the right. Add a task, switch the network off, add another, then switch it back on. The log shows what the real app does at each step. Chapter 4 explains every line of it.

You already know this shape from mobile work. The manifest is the web's `Info.plist` / `AndroidManifest.xml`. The service worker is a background isolate with no UI access. IndexedDB is the on-device database. Push goes through APNs and FCM, the same services native apps use.
The phone is a simulation that runs inside this page with example tasks. The real app, with a real service worker, is in the Build the app chapter.
How the pieces fit
The service worker is the centre of the design. Once it is installed, every request the page makes passes through it first, and it decides whether to answer from the cache, from the network, or both.

A service worker is a JavaScript file the browser runs in the background, separate from your page. It sits between your app and the network. Every request the page makes reaches the worker first, and the worker decides how to answer. That is what makes offline possible.

items: Intercept requests (`fetch` event).
Read and write Cache Storage and IndexedDB.
Receive push messages and show notifications.
Run when no tab is open (push, background sync).
Touch the DOM, `window` or `localStorage`.
Stay alive. The browser stops it after about 30 seconds of idle and restarts it for the next event, so global variables are lost.
Run on plain HTTP (except `localhost`).

The page loads from the network as usual and calls `register()`.
`install` runs. The worker downloads the app shell into a cache.
There is no older worker, so it activates straight away.
`clients.claim()` makes it control the page that is already open. Without that call, control starts on the next page load.
On the next visit the browser re-downloads `sw.js`. If even one byte differs, it is a new worker.
The new worker installs into a new cache while the old one keeps serving the old files.
It waits. Two versions of your code never run in the same tab.
When all old tabs close, or the user accepts your "Reload" prompt, it activates and deletes the old cache.

items: **Putting `sw.js` in a subfolder.** A worker at `/js/sw.js` controls only `/js/`. Serve it from the root.
**Caching `sw.js` itself for a long time.** Send it with `Cache-Control: no-cache`. Browsers cap the HTTP cache for the worker script at 24 hours anyway, but a day-long stale worker is still painful.
**Keeping state in a global variable.** The worker is stopped and restarted often. Persist to IndexedDB or the Cache.
**Changing a cached file without changing `VERSION`.** The worker file is byte-identical, so the browser sees no update and users keep the old file.
**Calling `respondWith()` after an `await`.** It must be called synchronously inside the event handler.

A caching strategy is the rule a service worker follows to answer one request: look in the cache, ask the network, or both, and in which order. There are five classic rules. A real app uses several, one per kind of file.
**Time until the page gets a response**

Numbers come from a simple model (cache read 5 ms, the network delay you picked, a 2.5 second timeout for network first). They are not measurements of a real site. For scale, in the task app on this Mac a cache-first hit took 0.8 ms and a network call to the local server 1.8 ms (median of 30 requests in Chromium), so the 5 ms cache figure is cautious. A real network adds tens to thousands of milliseconds; a cache read does not change.

Cache only and network only need no helper. Cache only is `event.respondWith(caches.match(request))`. Network only is not calling `respondWith()` at all, which is what the task app does for `/api/` and for every non-GET request.

A fixed list of files stored during `install`, before the user needs them. This is the app shell. It guarantees that the second visit works offline. Keep it small: every byte is downloaded by every user on first visit.
Responses stored as the user browses, by the strategies above. It can grow without limit, so real apps cap it (for example, keep the 50 newest entries) and delete it by name when the version changes.

items: **Clone before you store.** A response body is a stream that can be read once. `cache.put(request, response.clone())` keeps the original for the page.
**Check `response.ok` before caching.** Otherwise a 404 or 500 page is saved and served forever.
**Only GET can be cached.** `cache.put` throws on a POST request.

**Be careful with cross-origin files.** A response fetched without CORS is "opaque": you cannot read its status, so you may cache an error, and Chrome counts each opaque entry as about 7 MB against your storage budget. Ask the other server for CORS headers, or host the file yourself.
**Never cache per-user responses under a shared URL** unless you clear the caches on logout. The next person to sign in on that device would see them.
**`cache.addAll` is all or nothing.** One 404 in the precache list fails the whole install.

lessons.title: Why retrying is safe: the server side

blocks.text: A request can reach the server while its response is lost on the way back. The client then sends it again. This is harmless only if the server treats a repeat as a no-op. The client creates the task id, and the server stores by that id.
server.jsfrom the app
Conflicts

The app uses **last write wins**: each task carries `updatedAt`, and the server ignores a change older than what it has. That is enough for one person on two devices. It silently loses an edit when two people change the same task while offline. The Advanced chapter lists the stronger options.

items: **Trusting `navigator.onLine`.** `true` only means a network interface is up. Hotel Wi-Fi with a login page reports online. The reliable test is whether the request succeeded.
**Ids made by the server.** An offline-created task then has no id until sync, and every reference to it must be rewritten. Use `crypto.randomUUID()` on the client.
**A POST that creates a row on every call.** Retries create duplicates. Use PUT by id, or send an idempotency key.
**Awaiting something else in the middle of a transaction.** An IndexedDB transaction closes itself when the event loop goes idle. Do all the store calls synchronously, as `withTx` does.

Push lets your server send a message to a user's device when your app is closed. The browser vendor runs a push service that holds a connection to the device. Your server hands the message to that service, the service delivers it, the browser starts your service worker, and the worker shows a notification.

**Run end to end on 13 November 2026** in Chrome 157 on macOS, in a clean profile with notifications allowed. The app subscribed with Google's push service, the server sent a reminder 5 seconds later with the tab closed, and the notification arrived with the right title, body and tag. A second push replaced the first instead of stacking. After unsubscribing, the next send got a "gone" answer and the server deleted the subscription. Still not run: tapping the notification (it is an operating-system banner a script cannot click), and push on a real iPhone.

items: **Notifications API** draws the banner. It works without any server.
**Push API** delivers a message from a server to the worker. It draws nothing.

**Subscription keys** (`p256dh`, `auth`): made by the browser, used by your server to encrypt the payload so the push service cannot read it.

Eleven steps take you from an empty folder to an installable task manager that works offline, syncs when the connection returns and sends reminders. There is no framework and no build tool, so nothing hides what the browser is doing.

questions.q: What makes a website a Progressive Web App?
questions.a: Three things working together: it is served over HTTPS, it has a web app manifest so the operating system can install it, and it has a service worker so it can load and work without a network. "Progressive" means it still works as a normal website in a browser that supports none of this.

questions.q: Is a PWA a different technology from a website?
questions.a: No. It is the same HTML, CSS and JavaScript at the same URL. The manifest and the service worker are additions. One codebase serves the browser tab and the installed app.

questions.q: Why does a PWA need HTTPS?
questions.a: A service worker can intercept and rewrite every request for its origin. Over plain HTTP, anyone on the network path could inject a worker and keep control of the site on that device. Browsers therefore allow workers only on secure origins, with localhost as the exception for development.

questions.q: What is the app shell?
questions.a: The minimum HTML, CSS and JavaScript needed to draw the app's frame: header, navigation, empty content area. It is cached during install so the app paints instantly and offline, and the data is filled in afterwards.

questions.q: When would you choose a native app over a PWA?
questions.a: When you need capabilities the web lacks on your target platform: home-screen widgets, Live Activities, background location, deep Bluetooth or NFC use on iPhone, heavy graphics, or App Store discovery and in-app purchase flows. Choose a PWA when reach by link, one codebase and instant updates matter more.

questions.q: Does a PWA work in a browser with no service worker support?
questions.a: Yes, if you build it progressively. Guard registration with a feature check. The app then behaves like an ordinary online website. The task app in this guide does exactly this.

questions.q: How do users find and install a PWA?
questions.a: From the browser: an install icon in Chrome's or Edge's address bar, a menu entry on Android, or Share then Add to Home Screen on iPhone. You can also show your own install button in Chromium, or list the app in Google Play and the Microsoft Store through a wrapper.

questions.q: What are the minimum manifest fields for Chrome to offer installation?
questions.a: A name or short_name, a start_url, icons including 192 and 512 pixel PNGs, and display set to standalone, fullscreen or minimal-ui. The page must be on HTTPS. A service worker is no longer required for the prompt.

questions.q: What is the difference between name and short_name?
questions.a: name is the full title, used in the install dialog and on the splash screen. short_name is used where space is tight, mainly under the home-screen icon. Keep short_name to about 12 characters.

questions.q: What does the display field control?
questions.a: How much browser UI the installed app shows. standalone removes the address bar and looks like a native app. fullscreen also hides the status bar. minimal-ui keeps a small set of navigation controls. browser opens a normal tab and makes the app not installable in Chrome.

questions.q: What is a maskable icon and why provide one?
questions.a: An icon designed to be cropped to any shape. The background fills the whole square and the artwork stays inside the central 80 percent circle. Without one, Android shrinks your normal icon and puts it on a white plate.

questions.q: Why set the id field?
questions.a: It is the app's identity. Without it the identity is derived from start_url, so changing the start URL later makes browsers treat the site as a new, separate app. Setting id lets you change start_url safely.

questions.q: What is scope and what happens outside it?
questions.a: scope is the set of URLs that count as part of the app. Navigating to a URL outside it, even on your own domain, opens a browser view on top of the app with an address bar.

questions.q: How does iPhone use the manifest?
questions.a: Safari reads name, start_url, display and theme colour from it, but takes the Home Screen icon from the apple-touch-icon link tag. From iOS 26 a site added to the Home Screen opens as a web app by default even with no manifest.

questions.q: What is the difference between theme_color and background_color?
questions.a: theme_color tints the status bar, title bar and task switcher. background_color fills the splash screen shown between tapping the icon and your first paint. Match background_color to your page background to avoid a flash.

questions.q: Can you change the app name or icon after users have installed it?
questions.a: Yes, by changing the manifest. Chromium checks for manifest changes periodically and applies them, sometimes after asking the user to confirm a new name or icon. On iPhone the user must remove and re-add the app.

questions.q: What is a service worker in one sentence?
questions.a: A script the browser runs in the background, separate from any page, that can intercept the site's network requests and respond to events such as push even when no tab is open.

questions.q: Describe the service worker life cycle.
questions.a: The page registers the script. The browser downloads it and fires install, where you precache files. If an older worker controls open pages, the new one waits. When it can take over it fires activate, where you delete old caches. After that it handles fetch, push and sync events, and is stopped whenever it is idle.

questions.q: Why does a new service worker wait instead of activating immediately?
questions.a: To guarantee that one page never runs against two versions of your code. A tab loaded with version 1 HTML might later request a script that version 2 no longer has. Waiting until old tabs are gone avoids that.

questions.q: What do skipWaiting and clients.claim do?
questions.a: skipWaiting lets a waiting worker activate at once, without waiting for old tabs to close. clients.claim makes an active worker take control of pages that are already open and were loaded without it. They solve different problems and are often used together.

questions.q: How does the browser decide that a service worker has been updated?
questions.a: On navigation to a page in scope, and at most every 24 hours of use, it re-fetches the worker script and anything it imports. If the bytes differ from the installed copy, it is a new worker and install runs.

questions.q: Why can't you keep state in a service worker's global variables?
questions.a: The browser terminates an idle worker after roughly 30 seconds and starts a fresh instance for the next event. Globals are reset each time. Anything that must persist goes into IndexedDB or the Cache.

questions.q: What is event.waitUntil for?
questions.a: It extends the life of the event until the promise you pass settles. Without it the browser may kill the worker while your asynchronous work, such as writing to a cache or showing a notification, is still running.

questions.q: What determines a service worker's scope?
questions.a: By default, the folder the script is served from. A worker at /app/sw.js controls /app/ and below. To control the whole site, serve it from the root. A wider scope needs the Service-Worker-Allowed response header.

questions.q: Can a service worker access the DOM or localStorage?
questions.a: No. It has no document and no window, and localStorage is synchronous so it is not exposed. It talks to pages with postMessage and stores data with IndexedDB and the Cache API.

questions.q: Why must event.respondWith be called synchronously?
questions.a: The browser decides whether the worker will handle the request as soon as the fetch handler returns. If respondWith has not been called by then, the request goes to the network as normal. You can pass it a promise, but the call itself cannot come after an await.

questions.q: A user reports they still see the old version a week after you deployed. What are the likely causes?
questions.a: The new worker is installed but waiting because the installed app was never fully closed and there is no update prompt. Or a precached file changed but the worker file did not, so no update was detected. Or sw.js itself is served with a long cache lifetime.

questions.q: How do you unregister a broken service worker for all users?
questions.a: Deploy a replacement sw.js at the same URL that calls skipWaiting in install and, in activate, deletes all caches, calls registration.unregister and reloads open clients. Browsers pick it up on the next visit because the script's bytes changed.

questions.q: Name the five classic caching strategies.
questions.a: Cache first, network first, stale while revalidate, cache only and network only.

questions.q: When is cache first the right choice?
questions.a: For files that do not change under the same URL: the versioned app shell, fonts, icons, and scripts or styles with a content hash in the filename. It is the fastest strategy and fully offline.

questions.q: When is network first the right choice, and what is its weakness?
questions.a: For content where fresh matters but stale is acceptable as a fallback, such as HTML pages or a feed. Its weakness is slow networks: the user waits for the request to fail before seeing the cached copy. A timeout fixes that.

questions.q: Explain stale while revalidate.
questions.a: Answer immediately from the cache, and at the same time fetch a fresh copy and store it for next time. The user gets speed now and content that is at most one visit old. It suits images, avatars and rarely changing configuration.

questions.q: What is the difference between precaching and runtime caching?
questions.a: Precaching stores a known list of files during install, before they are requested. Runtime caching stores responses as requests happen. Precache the shell; runtime-cache everything you cannot list in advance.

questions.q: Why must you clone a response before caching it?
questions.a: A response body is a stream that can be consumed once. If you put the response in the cache and also return it to the page, one of them gets an empty body. response.clone creates a second readable copy.

questions.q: What is an opaque response and why is it a problem?
questions.a: The result of a cross-origin request made without CORS. You cannot read its status, headers or body, so you cannot tell a 200 from a 500 before caching it. Chrome also pads each one to about 7 MB when counting storage use.

questions.q: How does the Cache API differ from the browser's HTTP cache?
questions.a: The HTTP cache is automatic and controlled by response headers; the browser may evict entries at any time. The Cache API is fully under your script's control: you decide what goes in, when it is read and when it is deleted, and it ignores cache headers.

questions.q: How do you invalidate cached files when you deploy?
questions.a: Put a version in the cache name, change it in the worker, and delete caches with other names during activate. Larger apps use hashed filenames and a build-generated precache list so each file is its own version.

questions.q: Should API responses be cached by the service worker?
questions.a: Read-only, non-personal responses can be, with network first or stale while revalidate. For data the user edits, an IndexedDB store is better: you can query it, update single records and track unsynced changes, none of which a response cache does.

questions.q: What happens if one file in cache.addAll returns a 404?
questions.a: The whole addAll rejects, nothing from that call is stored, the install event fails and the new worker is discarded. The previous worker keeps running. This is a safety feature: you never get a half-filled shell.

questions.q: What does local-first mean?
questions.a: The app reads and writes a database on the device as its primary source, and syncs with the server in the background. The UI never waits for the network, so it is instant online and fully usable offline.

questions.q: Why use IndexedDB instead of localStorage for app data?
questions.a: IndexedDB is asynchronous, holds structured objects and large amounts of data, supports indexes and transactions, and is available inside service workers. localStorage is synchronous, string-only, limited to a few megabytes and not available to workers.

questions.q: What is the outbox pattern?
questions.a: Every local change is also written to a queue of pending operations. A sync routine sends the queue to the server in order and removes each entry once the server confirms it. The queue survives restarts because it is stored in IndexedDB.

questions.q: Why write the data change and the outbox entry in one transaction?
questions.a: So they cannot diverge. If the app were killed between two separate writes, you could have a saved task with no queued change, and the server would never learn about it.

questions.q: What makes retrying a sync request safe?
questions.a: Idempotency. The client generates the record id and the server upserts by that id, or the request carries an idempotency key. Sending the same request twice then leaves the same result as sending it once.

questions.q: What is the Background Sync API and where does it work?
questions.a: The page registers a tag, and the browser fires a sync event in the service worker once it believes the device is online, even if the tab was closed. If the handler's promise rejects, the browser retries with backoff. It is implemented in Chromium browsers only.

questions.q: How do you sync on Safari and Firefox, which lack Background Sync?
questions.a: From the page: on load, on the online event, when the app returns to the foreground, and on a manual retry control. Use the same flush function, so Background Sync is an extra safety net where it exists.

questions.q: Why is navigator.onLine unreliable?
questions.a: It reports whether the device has a network interface that is up, not whether your server is reachable. Captive portals, a dead router or a server outage all report online. Treat a failed request as the real signal.

questions.q: How does last write wins handle conflicts, and what does it lose?
questions.a: Each record has a timestamp or version, and the newer write replaces the older. It is simple and fine for one user. When two people edit the same record offline, one edit is dropped without notice.

questions.q: Why should the client, not the server, create record ids?
questions.a: A record created offline needs an id immediately so that later edits and deletes can refer to it. A client-made UUID also makes the create request idempotent.

questions.q: Can browser storage be deleted without the user asking?
questions.a: Yes. Storage is best-effort unless persistence is granted, so the browser may evict it when the disk is nearly full. Safari also clears script-written storage for sites not used for 7 days, except apps on the Home Screen.

questions.q: What is the difference between the Push API and the Notifications API?
questions.a: The Push API delivers a message from a server to the service worker. The Notifications API displays a notification to the user. Push notifications use both: a push event arrives and its handler calls showNotification.

questions.q: Walk through subscribing a user to push.
questions.a: After a tap, request notification permission. Fetch your server's VAPID public key. Call pushManager.subscribe with userVisibleOnly true and that key. The browser returns a subscription with an endpoint URL and two keys. Send that object to your server and store it.

questions.q: What is VAPID?
questions.a: Voluntary Application Server Identification. Your server holds a key pair. The browser ties a subscription to the public key, and the server signs each push with the private key, so the push service accepts messages for that subscription only from you.

questions.q: Who runs the push service, and do you choose it?
questions.a: The browser vendor: Google's FCM for Chrome, Mozilla's service for Firefox, Apple's APNs for Safari. You do not choose. The endpoint URL in the subscription points to the right one, and all speak the same Web Push protocol.

questions.q: Why must every push show a notification?
questions.a: Browsers do not allow silent background wake-ups from the web, to protect battery and privacy. You declare this with userVisibleOnly true. Chrome shows a generic notification if you skip it; Safari revokes the subscription after a few silent pushes.

questions.q: What are the requirements for web push on iPhone?
questions.a: iOS or iPadOS 16.4 or later, the app added to the Home Screen and opened from there, and a permission request triggered by a user tap. In an ordinary Safari tab on iPhone the Push API is not available.

questions.q: The user tapped Block. What can you do?
questions.a: Nothing from code. requestPermission will return denied without showing a prompt. Show instructions for re-enabling notifications in browser or system settings, and avoid the situation by asking only after the user shows intent.

questions.q: How should the server react to a 410 Gone from the push service?
questions.a: Delete that subscription. 404 and 410 mean it has expired or the user unsubscribed, and it will never work again.

questions.q: How do you open the right screen when a notification is tapped?
questions.a: Put a URL in the notification's data. In notificationclick, close the notification, look for an open window of your app with clients.matchAll, focus and navigate it if found, otherwise call clients.openWindow with the URL.

questions.q: Is the push payload readable by the push service?
questions.a: No. The payload is encrypted on your server with keys from the subscription, and only the browser can decrypt it. The push service sees the endpoint and some headers such as TTL and urgency.

questions.q: How do you keep content out of the notch and home-indicator area?
questions.a: Add viewport-fit=cover to the viewport meta tag so the page may draw edge to edge, then pad your header and footer with env(safe-area-inset-top) and the other inset variables.

questions.q: How do you detect that the app is running installed rather than in a tab?
questions.a: In CSS and JavaScript, the display-mode: standalone media query. On older iOS versions, navigator.standalone is also true.

questions.q: What is beforeinstallprompt?
questions.a: A Chromium-only event fired when the app meets the install criteria. Call preventDefault, keep the event, and later call its prompt method from a tap to show the install dialog. Safari and Firefox do not fire it.

questions.q: Why does an iPhone zoom in when an input is focused, and how do you stop it?
questions.a: Safari zooms when the input's font size is under 16 pixels. Set inputs to 16 pixels or larger. Do not disable zoom globally.

questions.q: What replaces the browser's back and reload buttons in standalone mode?
questions.a: Nothing, so you must provide them. Give every screen in-app navigation, and build an update prompt or refresh control, since there is no reload button.

questions.q: How do you show an unread count on the app icon?
questions.a: navigator.setAppBadge(count), and clearAppBadge to remove it. It works in Chromium on desktop and in installed web apps on iOS 16.4 and later. Android shows a dot based on notifications instead.

questions.q: Compare the three ways to roll out a service worker update.
questions.a: Wait for all tabs to close: safe but slow. Call skipWaiting in install: fast, but open pages may mix old HTML with new assets. Prompt the user, then skipWaiting and reload on controllerchange: safe and timely, at the cost of a little code.

questions.q: What is navigation preload?
questions.a: A feature that lets the browser start the network request for a page navigation while the service worker is still booting, instead of after. The worker reads the result from event.preloadResponse. It removes worker start-up time from network-first page loads.

questions.q: What does Workbox give you over a hand-written worker?
questions.a: Tested implementations of the strategies, a build step that generates the precache list with revision hashes, cache expiration, a background-sync queue with a fallback, and routing helpers. You write configuration instead of plumbing.

questions.q: How much can a PWA store?
questions.a: It varies by browser and free disk space. Chromium allows an origin up to about 60 percent of the disk. Call navigator.storage.estimate to read the actual usage and quota at run time, and design for writes that can fail.

questions.q: How do you make stored data survive storage pressure?
questions.a: Call navigator.storage.persist. If granted, the browser will not evict the origin's data automatically. Chrome decides silently based on signals such as being installed; Firefox asks the user.

questions.q: How do you debug a service worker on a real phone?
questions.a: Android: connect by USB and use chrome://inspect on the computer. iPhone: enable Web Inspector in Safari settings, connect to a Mac and use Safari's Develop menu, which lists Home Screen apps and their workers.

questions.q: What security risks does a service worker add?
questions.a: A script injected through XSS could register a malicious worker that persists after the hole is fixed. Cached responses can leak between users on a shared device. Mitigate with a strict Content-Security-Policy, by clearing caches on logout and by keeping a kill-switch worker ready.

questions.q: How do you publish a PWA to Google Play?
questions.a: With a Trusted Web Activity: a small Android app that opens your PWA full screen in Chrome's engine. Bubblewrap or PWABuilder generates the project, and a Digital Asset Links file on your site proves ownership so no browser bar is shown.

questions.q: Why might a PWA behave differently in Chrome on iPhone than in Chrome on Android?
questions.a: On iPhone, browsers are built on Apple's WebKit engine, so Chrome there has Safari's capabilities and limits: no Background Sync, no beforeinstallprompt, push only when installed.

questions.q: Your offline test passes in DevTools but fails on a train. Why might that be?
questions.a: DevTools Offline fails requests instantly. A real weak connection makes them hang for a long time. A network-first strategy without a timeout will wait on every request. Add timeouts and test with throttling as well as full offline.

questions.q: How would you measure whether offline support is working for real users?
questions.a: Log, in IndexedDB, events such as launches served from cache, outbox size and age, and sync failures, and upload them when online. Watch the age of the oldest outbox entry and the share of clients on the latest worker version.
